britannica-1911-sutlej:
Sutlej, a river of India, is given a course entry in the 1911 Britannica as one of the Five Rivers of the Punjab. It rises in Tibet near the Manasarowar lakes, some 15,200 feet up. From there it threads Himalayan gorges, crosses the Simla hill states, and enters Hoshiarpur. Then it flows through the Punjab plains and takes in the Beas.

Below its meeting with the Chenab the whole stream bears the name Panjnad till it joins the Indus, after a course of 900 miles. In the time of Ranjit Singh the Sutlej marked the line between Sikh and British lands. The states south of it still bear the title Cis-Sutlej. The Sirhind canal draws off the cold season flow at Rupar.
nasa-tm-19700016380-flight-performance-o:
Nick E. Samanich and Richard R. Burley of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a 1970 propulsion conference in San Diego. It reports flight performance for two jet nozzle types at transonic speeds. The types are the auxiliary inlet ejector nozzle and the conical plug nozzle.

A nozzle shapes the exhaust that pushes a jet plane forward. The authors note that nozzle results can change with the way the nozzle is fitted to the airframe. They studied each nozzle in the same installation to keep the comparison fair. Findings like these guided the choice of nozzles for fast aircraft.
nasa-tm-19700025285-evasive-maneuver-sub:
An evasive maneuver after ejection from the S-IVB stage is the subject of this Houston internal note, dated June 13, 1969. It concerns the Apollo craft in Earth orbit. Once free, the command module and lunar module had to move clear of the spent stage, which would later be fired again.

The note works through the limits the maneuver had to respect. The small thrusters needed a minimum burn time, yet total maneuvering was to stay as low as possible. The plan had to hold regardless of lift-off date and keep a safe gap at stage reignition. Other limits cover side position at ignition, time spent in the side zone, and avoiding contact again if reignition never came.
